title: Hardware noise-based random generators deviate from perfect randomness

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Hardware noise-based random generators deviate from perfect randomness

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Devices that generate randomness by amplifying microscopic environmental noise (spark gaps, vacuum tubes, semiconductor diodes) have consistently been found to produce output with significant deviations from perfect randomness, because the sampling device relaxes only gradually and because the environment itself has correlations.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But despite such sensitivity to microscopic effects, what has consistently been found in practice is that the output from such devices has significant deviations from perfect randomness.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 7, “Mechanisms in Programs and Nature”; section “Randomness from the Environment” (from p. 301), p. 303. Scope: physical random number generators based on electronic or other environmental noise

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch07-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Randomness deviations have standard tests and some public physical-generator outputs exist. The “consistently” claim across historical device classes and its causal explanation exceed the coverage and rawness of current public data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Collect existing raw bitstreams from documented electronic-noise generators and test bias, autocorrelation, spectral structure, and entropy with correction disabled. Relate deviations to measured recovery times and environmental correlations, comparing against quantum and algorithmic controls.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Historical spark-gap and diode records are sparse.

Detected deviations do not uniquely identify the proposed causes.

Public streams often include conditioning that removes raw-device deviations.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Deviation from perfect randomness is operational in the NIST and TestU01 batteries, and published evaluations of noise-based generators are real but scattered. Those evaluations over-represent modern diodes relative to the spark gaps and vacuum tubes named in the text, and they rarely separate relaxation from environmental correlation. The sample can test a proxy for consistently; it does not cover the historical class.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Run a standard randomness battery on bitstreams from noise-amplifying hardware, and where the device physics is documented, test dead time and environmental correlation as causes. Systematic battery failures support deviations; a large public set of historically relevant devices that pass would challenge consistently.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Open streams cover modern semiconductor devices far better than spark gaps and vacuum tubes.

A failed battery shows a deviation; a passed battery does not prove perfect randomness.

Dead time and environmental correlation are confounded in most published bitstreams.
